title: The body's matter
hookLine: the senses, the body's life, its heat, its nourishment

cards: What's the difference between your hand and the table it's resting on? By yesterday's account, both are made of the same four great elements. Both are hard, both hold together, both have a temperature, both press.
Yet one of them can feel the other, and the other can't. One gets warm from the inside, gets hungry, heals a cut. The table does none of that.
So the manual keeps going past the four, into the kinds of matter that belong only to a living body.

teach.b: Start with the senses. In the Abhidhamma, the eye that sees isn't the eyeball. It's a fine, sensitive matter inside it, ready to be struck by color.
The same sensitive matter sits in the ear, the nose, the tongue and the whole surface of the body: five doors where the world gets in. A table has none. Next, life.

teach.h: THE LIFE FACULTY KEEPS IT GOING.
teach.b: The manual names a kind of matter called the life faculty, which keeps the other living matter going, the way a caretaker keeps a garden watered.
When it stops, the four great elements are still there, but the body is no longer alive. Then heat.
Here temperature is one of the forces that keeps producing matter, moment after moment: warmth in a living body is part of what keeps it being made. And nourishment.
Food, in this system, carries a subtle nutritive essence, and that essence keeps producing matter too.

teach.h: HEAT AND FOOD KEEP MAKING MATTER.
teach.b: So the manual names four things that keep matter arising: past kamma, the mind, temperature and food. A table gets only one. A living body gets all four.
Notice what the list never adds: a fifth thing, a soul or a self.
A living body is matter held up by more conditions, not matter with someone hiding inside.
In one sutta the Buddha says the world, its arising and its ending are found in this fathom-long body, with its perception and mind. The Abhidhamma takes him at his word and starts measuring.

how: Abhidhamma students learn the kinds of matter found only in living bodies, such as the sense organs' sensitive matter and the life faculty, and some meditation teachers in the Theravada tradition guide students to feel warmth and other qualities in the body directly.

o: the four elements that every object shares
the soul that lives on inside the body
the kinds of matter only a living body has

games.q: the body's matter: tap the pairs.

s: in the Abhidhamma, the eye that sees is the eyeball
it's a fine, sensitive matter inside the eye, ready to be struck by color.
the manual names kamma, mind, temperature and food as producers of matter
a living body gets all four; a table gets only one.
the manual adds a soul to explain why a body is alive
it adds no self; a living body is matter held up by more conditions.

games.q: a living hand and a table are both made of the four great elements. what does the manual say makes the difference?
o: a self hiding in the hand
more kinds of matter and more conditions: sense doors, life, heat, food
games.why: the manual lists sensitive matter, the life faculty, and matter kept arising by kamma, mind, temperature and food. it never adds a self.

practice: Bring your attention to your hands and notice their warmth, without deciding whether it's pleasant.
Then let attention move to the belly, the chest, the back of the neck, and rest wherever there's warmth: the body doing its work, moment by moment, without your help.
If you like, place one palm over the other and feel heat meeting heat.

wordCard.voice: The body's matter. The sense doors, the life faculty, and the heat and food that keep a living body being made. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: the life faculty, the kind of matter that keeps the other living matter going.

carryVoice: Your line: living matter. A hand and a table share the same four elements, and only one of them can feel. See you tomorrow.
